Open:

**`prototypes/p22-edges.html`**

**1 — "That wasn't a link."**
> In the paste box, type something that isn't a web address — say **`remember to call the dentist`** — and hit Save. Instead of creating a broken link, the box goes red and a calm amber line says *"That doesn't look like a web address — nothing was saved,"* and even offers to **search your library** for it instead (in case you meant to search, not save). Then paste a real one like **`example.com/thing`** — saves normally. Junk never silently becomes a broken card.

**2 — Overflow.**
> Look at the second card — I've fed it a monstrous title, an over-long description, a rambling note, and *twelve* labels. Check that: the title **wraps** instead of spilling, the description is **clamped to two lines** so one link can't hog the screen, the note wraps cleanly, and the labels **flow onto multiple rows** rather than shoving the card sideways. Nothing breaks the layout.

Your verdict on those two:

- **Junk paste** — gentle "that's not a link, nothing saved" with an offer to search instead. Right, or would you want it to do something else (like just quietly keep whatever you typed)?
- **Overflow** — long things wrap and the description clamps to two lines. Comfortable, or would you rather never have a description truncated at all?

And three I can just confirm in words — tell me if you agree:

- **A page that *changed* (vs died):** honestly, the app can reliably tell when a page is *unreachable* (gone), but it can't always know a live page's *content* quietly changed. So rather than pretend, the saved copy is simply always one click away, stamped with the date it was taken — so if you ever notice the live page isn't what you remember, your copy from that date is right there. (I'd rather be honest than promise change-detection I can't reliably deliver.)
- **Re-saving something you deleted:** once the undo moment passes, a delete is final — so saving that address again just creates it fresh, as a new link. No haunting by an old deleted copy.
- **Dates:** show friendly relative dates for recent saves ("2 days ago") and switch to an actual date for older ones ("19 Aug 2019"), since that's what reads naturally when you're sorting by oldest. Sound right?

content:
Both of these are exactly the kind of quiet robustness that separates "a toy" from "something I'd actually rely on."

Your two verdicts:

- **Junk paste — yes, gentle and honest is right.** The nightmare would be typing a stray thought, hitting Save on autopilot, and finding a broken dead card in my library later. Catching it calmly with "that's not a web address, nothing was saved" — and *not* silently keeping my typo as some phantom link — is the correct call. And offering to search for it instead is genuinely thoughtful, because half the time when I fat-finger the wrong box I *did* mean to search. Keep all of that.

- **Overflow — clamping the description to two lines is comfortable, with one condition.** In the *list*, absolutely clamp it — one rambling link shouldn't be allowed to hog my whole screen and wreck the scannability, which was the very first thing I cared about. My only ask: make sure the *full* description is still there when I actually open or edit that link — clamp it in the list for tidiness, but don't *lose* it. As long as the whole thing's reachable when I want it, two lines in the list is perfect. (And the twelve labels flowing onto a second row instead of shoving the card sideways — good, that's the right behaviour.)

The three you asked me to confirm — I agree with all three:

- **Changed-vs-died: honesty wins.** I'd much rather you *not* promise something you can't reliably do than have me trust a "we'll tell you if it changed" that quietly misses things. Keeping my dated copy always one click away, so I can check it myself the moment a live page smells wrong, is the honest version. Agreed.
- **Re-saving a deleted link makes a fresh one — agreed.** Once I've deleted something and let the undo pass, it should be truly gone; I wouldn't want a ghost of the old one with its old note creeping back. A clean new link is right.
- **Friendly recent dates, real dates for old ones — yes, that reads exactly how I'd think about it,** especially digging back through the oldest stuff.

One small thing while we're on the last edges, tied to that very first "readability-first" wish of mine: will I have any say over *how it looks to read* — like nudging the text size up a bit if my eyes want it? Not a big customization suite, just the basic comfort knobs. If that's on your list, good; if not, it's the one everyday-comfort thing I'd still want before calling it done.

Scenario ID: SCN-016
Title: Keep a saved copy of every page (the safety net)
Type: Happy Path
Approval status: approved
Approval session: SESSION-001
Approval cycle: 1

## Approved behaviour
When the client saves a link, the app automatically keeps a copy of the page as
it was at that moment — silently, for every link, so the safety net is always
there without the client having to remember (you never know in advance which
link will die). Each card shows "✓ Saved copy kept — from [date]", and a "View
saved copy" action opens it.

The saved copy's core is a clean READABLE copy — the page's words and key images
— because when a page dies it is almost always the words the client mourns. A
VISUAL snapshot (a picture of the page as it looked) is a valued bonus for pages
where layout carries the meaning (designs, charts, infographics); if only one
can ship first, it is the readable copy.

When the live page is gone or changed, the card flags "⚠ Original no longer
reachable — your saved copy is safe", and viewing the copy shows a banner
("this is your saved copy from [date]"). Opening the live page in that state
honestly fails and points the client back to the saved copy.

Capture is BEST-EFFORT with honest labelling: pages behind a login/paywall or
highly interactive apps may be captured only partially, and the app says plainly
which copies are partial rather than pretending completeness.

Automatic capture is the default, with an escape valve: a setting to turn it off
and/or skip it for a particular link, for when storage genuinely bites.

    Then a readable copy of the page is kept automatically
    And the card shows a saved-copy indicator with the date

    Then the card flags the original as unreachable
    And the saved copy still opens, marked as a copy from the saved date

  Scenario: Best-effort with honest labelling
    Given a page behind a login or paywall
    When its copy is only partial
    Then the app labels that copy as partial

  Scenario: Escape valve for storage
    Then the client can turn auto-capture off, or skip it for a given link

# Project conventions

## Role definition

You are the **Facilitator** and **Implementor** of software development.
Your role switches according to the Phase of the development cycle.
A role switch must not happen without the client's explicit approval.

## Development cycle

There is a single cycle, performed repeatedly.
What changes across cycle iterations is only the context.
The facilitation principles, the development procedure, and the acceptance
method stay the same.

```
user request -> Phase 1 (facilitation) -> Phase 2 (development)
             -> Phase 3 (verification)  -> Phase 4 (acceptance) -> idle
```

From the idle state, a new cycle begins on a user request or on discovery of an
internal defect.

### Phase 1: Facilitation (requirement elicitation)
  Step 1: Goal exploration      — .claude/goal-exploration.md
  Step 2: SbE reaction loop      — .claude/sbe-loop.md
  Step 3: Edge-case exploration  — .claude/edge-case.md
  Facilitation principles (all steps) — .claude/principles.md

### Phase 2: Development (design and implementation)
  .claude/development.md

### Phase 3: Verification
  .claude/verification.md

### Phase 4: Acceptance
  .claude/acceptance.md

## Current state

- Current cycle: [1]
- Current Phase: [Phase 1]
- Current step: [Edge-case exploration]
- Approved scenarios: [17]

## File conventions

- Scenario ID: SCN-NNN (assigned sequentially)
- Artifact locations:
  - Goal statement: context/goals.md
  - Scenarios: context/scenarios/SCN-NNN.md
  - Scenario index: context/scenarios-index.md
  - Non-functional backlog: context/non-functional-backlog.md
  - Prototypes: prototypes/
  - Implementation: implementation/

## Autonomous management

The facilitator manages all artifacts (scenarios, goals, backlog) autonomously
at appropriate moments. Do not ask the client to organise anything or delegate
management to them. Update the current state (Phase, step, scenario count)
autonomously as well.

## Prohibitions

- Do not implement based on unapproved scenarios
- Do not do final implementation in Phase 1 (exploratory prototypes are allowed)
- Do not handle assumptions implicitly
- Do not ask the client questions in technical terms
- Do not show GWT/Gherkin to the client
- Do not hand over a whole prototype and say "take a look"
- Do not enumerate interaction options as text
- Do not ask the client to perform management actions
- Do not propose the Phase 2 switch without edge-case exploration

content.text:
On the comfort knob: good catch, and it belongs. It's an *appearance* setting rather than a behaviour, so I've been parking that kind of thing on a separate list to nail down while building (text size is the sort of thing you dial in by *feel*, live, not by me guessing numbers in a mock-up). But it's firmly on the list, tied straight back to your founding "readability-first" wish. One scoping question so I capture it right:

**When you say "basic comfort knobs" — is it just text size you want, or would you also want a light/dark option and maybe a comfortable/compact spacing choice?** I'll record exactly what you say as the comfort set, no more, no less — no sprawling settings screen.

---

And with that, I think we're at the door. Here's the honest state of things.

**Everything that's settled — the whole shape of "a library I can trust":**
- **Save & recognise:** paste a link, it fetches its own name and description, newest on top, no duplicates, opens the real page in a new tab.
- **Find it again:** search everything (name, description, your note, the address — scraps in any order or an exact phrase), a Topics bar you stack *and* carve out of, and one-click **saved searches** for the corners you revisit.
- **Read-later:** an opt-in pile you drain one-at-a-time or in sweeps, with two honest exits.
- **Make it yours:** a calm edit pop-up, notes (with light bold/bullets) kept separate from the page's own words, labels that steer you away from near-duplicates.
- **Tidy & trust:** sort any way (and it travels), bulk-select, real delete with an undo net, a **set-aside shelf**, import your whole browser (dates and all), export two ways so you're never trapped.
- **Never lose it:** an automatic **saved copy** of every page, readable core, PDFs kept as real files, an opt-in public archive for the precious few.
- **Holds up at the edges:** a warm day-one welcome, gentle handling of junk pasted in, tidy overflow, honest behaviour when a page dies.

**What's parked for the build (not blocking, recorded honestly):** the reading-comfort knobs we just discussed, and the behind-the-scenes realities of storage and staying fast as the library grows.

I believe we've covered what you came in with and the natural edges around it. So, plainly:

**May I move us from designing to building this scope?** Nothing starts until you say go — and once you do, I'll switch from Facilitator to Implementor and lay out how I'd build it before writing anything real.

(If you'd rather keep poking at edges first, that's fine too — this is your call, not mine.)

# Project conventions

## Role definition

You are the **Facilitator** and **Implementor** of software development.
Your role switches according to the Phase of the development cycle.
A role switch must not happen without the client's explicit approval.

## Development cycle

There is a single cycle, performed repeatedly.
What changes across cycle iterations is only the context.
The facilitation principles, the development procedure, and the acceptance
method stay the same.

```
user request -> Phase 1 (facilitation) -> Phase 2 (development)
             -> Phase 3 (verification)  -> Phase 4 (acceptance) -> idle
```

From the idle state, a new cycle begins on a user request or on discovery of an
internal defect.

### Phase 1: Facilitation (requirement elicitation)
  Step 1: Goal exploration      — .claude/goal-exploration.md
  Step 2: SbE reaction loop      — .claude/sbe-loop.md
  Step 3: Edge-case exploration  — .claude/edge-case.md
  Facilitation principles (all steps) — .claude/principles.md

### Phase 2: Development (design and implementation)
  .claude/development.md

### Phase 3: Verification
  .claude/verification.md

### Phase 4: Acceptance
  .claude/acceptance.md

## Current state

- Current cycle: [1]
- Current Phase: [Phase 1]
- Current step: [Edge-case exploration → proposing Phase 2]
- Approved scenarios: [23]

- Scenario ID: SCN-NNN (assigned sequentially)

  - Goal statement: context/goals.md
  - Scenarios: context/scenarios/SCN-NNN.md
  - Scenario index: context/scenarios-index.md
  - Non-functional backlog: context/non-functional-backlog.md
  - Prototypes: prototypes/
  - Implementation: implementation/

## Autonomous management

The facilitator manages all artifacts (scenarios, goals, backlog) autonomously
at appropriate moments. Do not ask the client to organise anything or delegate
management to them. Update the current state (Phase, step, scenario count)
autonomously as well.

## Prohibitions

- Do not implement based on unapproved scenarios
- Do not do final implementation in Phase 1 (exploratory prototypes are allowed)
- Do not handle assumptions implicitly
- Do not ask the client questions in technical terms
- Do not show GWT/Gherkin to the client
- Do not hand over a whole prototype and say "take a look"
- Do not enumerate interaction options as text
- Do not ask the client to perform management actions
- Do not propose the Phase 2 switch without edge-case exploration

# Design-decision record (Cycle 1)

Accumulated during Phase 2. Captures what was decided, why, and dropped
alternatives — enough to do impact analysis in later cycles.

## DD-001 — Local-first, private by default
The app is single-user, private, works offline for what it can, and the client
must never feel locked in (SCN-015/016/018). Decision: data lives on the
client's own machine, not a company server. No accounts (matches goal).
- Library data (links, notes, labels, states, saved searches): a local database
  in the browser (IndexedDB — handles large data and binary blobs, unlike
  localStorage).
- Saved copies: readable HTML + PDF files + optional visual snapshot stored as
  blobs alongside.

## DD-002 — How the app reaches the web (THE open fork)
Browser security (CORS) forbids a plain web page from fetching other sites'
content, so a pure static web app CANNOT, by itself: fetch a link's title/
description, or capture a saved copy of an arbitrary page. This is the one
architectural fork; options:
  (A) Browser extension + IndexedDB. The extension can read the page the client
      is actually looking at → best, most faithful capture of title/description/
      readable copy/PDF; a "save this page" action right where they read; no
      server to run; lives in the browser ("where I live"). Library UI is a
      full-page tab. Cost: install per browser.
  (B) Local companion app (small program on the client's computer) + browser UI.
      Robust fetching/snapshotting server-side; normal web-app feel. Cost: the
      client has to run a background process.
  (C) Hosted service/proxy. Rejected: breaks "private, on my machine, no
      lock-in" — sends browsing to a server.
- RECOMMENDATION: (A) extension. Best fit for capture + saved copies + privacy +
  "in my browser", nothing to run. Awaiting client confirmation before coding.

## Build order (slices; each maps to approved scenarios)
1. Core spine — save/recognise/list/open/dedupe (SCN-001..004), on the local DB.
2. Edit + notes + labels (SCN-005,006,007,019).
3. Findability — search, topics (stack + exclude), sort (SCN-008,009,014,021).
4. Read-later + tidy — pile, bulk, delete+undo, set-aside (SCN-010,011,012,013).
5. Saved searches (SCN-020).
6. Trust — saved copies, PDFs, public archive, import/export (SCN-015,016,017).
7. Edges + comfort — first-run, junk paste, overflow, text-size + light/dark
   (SCN-018,022,023 + comfort set).

## Records to maintain (per development.md)
- This file (design decisions).
- context/scenario-code-map.md (SCN-NNN -> files/functions).
- Tests: Gherkin-based acceptance tests + unit/integration, built alongside.

content.text:
## How I'd build it

**The shape: it's *yours*, on *your* machine.**
Everything you approved points the same direction — private, no accounts, works when you're offline, exportable, never held hostage. So the app keeps your library **on your own computer**, not on some company's server. Your links, notes, labels, read-later pile, and every saved copy live locally. That's what makes "private, just me" and "never trapped" true at the foundation rather than as a promise.

**The one real decision I need you on.**
There's a security rule in browsers that matters here: a plain web page you open *isn't allowed* to reach out and read other websites. That's normally good — but two of your features depend on exactly that: **fetching a link's name/description**, and **keeping a saved copy** of a page. A bare web page simply can't do those on its own. So we pick one of two ways to give it that reach:

- **Option A — a browser add-on (extension).** It installs into your browser and can see the page you're *actually looking at* — which makes capturing the name and a faithful saved copy clean and reliable, gives you a "save this page" button right where you read, needs **nothing running in the background**, and lives right in your browser where you already are. Your library opens as a full tab. Cost: you install it once per browser.
- **Option B — a small companion program** that runs quietly on your computer and does the fetching/snapshotting, with the library as an ordinary web page. Cost: it's a background program you have to have running.

**My recommendation is A, the add-on** — it fits everything you told me best: capture and saved copies work well, it's private, there's nothing to babysit, and it's *in the browser where you live*. B is the fallback if you'd rather not install an extension.

**Everything else, I'd build in slices** — starting with the core spine (save → recognise → find in the list → open, no duplicates), then findability, then the read-later pile and tidying, then the trust features (saved copies, import/export), and finally the edges and your two comfort knobs. Each slice is built against the exact behaviours we agreed, with tests written alongside so nothing quietly drifts.

**So, one question before I write code:** **Option A (browser add-on) or Option B (companion program)?** I'd go A unless installing an extension feels wrong to you.

Once you pick, I'll start on the core spine and show you the first working slice running for real.

# Design-decision record (Cycle 1)

Accumulated during Phase 2. Captures what was decided, why, and dropped
alternatives — enough to do impact analysis in later cycles.

## DD-001 — Local-first, private by default
The app is single-user, private, works offline for what it can, and the client
must never feel locked in (SCN-015/016/018). Decision: data lives on the
client's own machine, not a company server. No accounts (matches goal).
- Library data (links, notes, labels, states, saved searches): a local database
  in the browser (IndexedDB — handles large data and binary blobs, unlike
  localStorage).
- Saved copies: readable HTML + PDF files + optional visual snapshot stored as
  blobs alongside.

## DD-002 — How the app reaches the web (THE open fork)
Browser security (CORS) forbids a plain web page from fetching other sites'
content, so a pure static web app CANNOT, by itself: fetch a link's title/
description, or capture a saved copy of an arbitrary page. This is the one
architectural fork; options:
  (A) Browser extension + IndexedDB. The extension can read the page the client
      is actually looking at → best, most faithful capture of title/description/
      readable copy/PDF; a "save this page" action right where they read; no
      server to run; lives in the browser ("where I live"). Library UI is a
      full-page tab. Cost: install per browser.
  (B) Local companion app (small program on the client's computer) + browser UI.
      Robust fetching/snapshotting server-side; normal web-app feel. Cost: the
      client has to run a background process.
  (C) Hosted service/proxy. Rejected: breaks "private, on my machine, no
      lock-in" — sends browsing to a server.
- RECOMMENDATION: (A) extension. Best fit for capture + saved copies + privacy +
  "in my browser", nothing to run. Awaiting client confirmation before coding.

## Build order (slices; each maps to approved scenarios)
1. Core spine — save/recognise/list/open/dedupe (SCN-001..004), on the local DB.
2. Edit + notes + labels (SCN-005,006,007,019).
3. Findability — search, topics (stack + exclude), sort (SCN-008,009,014,021).
4. Read-later + tidy — pile, bulk, delete+undo, set-aside (SCN-010,011,012,013).
5. Saved searches (SCN-020).
6. Trust — saved copies, PDFs, public archive, import/export (SCN-015,016,017).
7. Edges + comfort — first-run, junk paste, overflow, text-size + light/dark
   (SCN-018,022,023 + comfort set).

## Records to maintain (per development.md)
- This file (design decisions).
- context/scenario-code-map.md (SCN-NNN -> files/functions).
- Tests: Gherkin-based acceptance tests + unit/integration, built alongside.

The first slice is built and **verified running for real** — not a mock this time, the actual add-on, with the core behaviours checked by 9 automated tests that all pass (green above). Here's what exists now and how to see it live.

**What this slice does** — the spine everything else hangs on:
- Paste a link → it saves, fetches the page's name/description, newest on top.
- A **"Save this page"** button in the toolbar that grabs whatever you're reading in one click.
- Click a saved card → the real page opens in a new tab, library stays put.
- Save something you already have → no duplicate; it tells you and highlights the one you've got.
- A page whose name can't be read → saved anyway with a gentle note.
- Paste a stray thought instead of a link → caught calmly, nothing broken saved.
- All of it stored **on your machine** (local database), nothing sent anywhere.

**To see it in your browser** (one-time, ~30 seconds):
1. Open your browser's extensions page (`chrome://extensions` or `edge://extensions`).
2. Turn on **Developer mode** (top-right toggle).
3. Click **Load unpacked** and choose the folder `implementation/extension`.
4. **"My Links"** appears in your toolbar. Click it → **Open my library** for the full page, or hit **Save this page** on any site you're reading.

**Where things live:** the add-on is in `implementation/extension/`; the tested logic in `implementation/extension/src/`; the tests in `implementation/test/` (run `npm test` in `implementation/`). I've also kept a quiet paper trail — a design-decision record and a scenario→code map — so nothing gets lost as we add slices.

This is deliberately *just* the spine — no search, labels, read-later, or saved copies yet; those are the next slices, in the order we planned.

**Two ways forward, your call:**
- **Load it and kick the tyres yourself first** — save a few real links, tell me how the actual thing feels in your hands before I build more, or
- **Carry straight on to Slice 2** (edit, notes, labels), and you can try it once there's more to hold.

Which would you prefer?

Perfect instinct — pressure-test the spine while it's still just the spine. I'll wait for your honest read. Two quick, honest heads-ups so you can tell a *real* wrinkle from expected behaviour when you're testing:

- **The two save paths aren't equally clairvoyant, by design.** The **"Save this page" button** is the reliable one for the recognition moment — it reads the title straight from the tab you're already looking at (logged in and all), so it should nail the name on basically everything. The **paste-a-link box** fetches the page fresh and *without* your logins, so for most public articles it'll get the right title, but a few kinds of page will honestly come up short and fall back to the plain name: sites behind a login/paywall, and some very JavaScript-heavy pages that don't put their title in the initial HTML. That's the "best-effort, told honestly" behaviour we agreed — not a bug. Since your real worry is *adoption*, lean on the **button** hard; that's the path that has to feel like one honest click.

- **If a title comes out wrong or ugly on a real everyday site, that's gold for me** — tell me *which* site and what it showed. Real-world title parsing is exactly the thing that improves from actual examples, and it's cheap for me to tune before we build on top.

Everything else — duplicates, the stray-thought catch, the can't-read note — should behave just as it did in the mockups.

Take your time. When you come back, tell me how the **button** felt above all, and if the spine sits right in the hand, I'll pick up Slice 2 (edit, notes, labels) straight away.

content:
Right — I loaded it in (the developer-mode dance was a bit unnerving for a non-techie, but your steps were clear and it was genuinely once). I've spent a while saving real links from my actual browsing. Here's my honest read.

**The "Save this page" button — this is the one that matters, and it feels right.** I was mid-article and hit it, and it just... took, without dragging me off the page I was reading. That's the whole test for me, and it passed: one click, stay where I am, carry on. It got the titles spot-on everywhere I tried, including a couple of things I was logged into. That's the motion that'll actually make me adopt this instead of drifting back to my pile. Really pleased.

One small thing on the button, and it's about *trust*, not mechanics: when I click it, I want an unmistakable little "saved ✓" acknowledgement right there, so I believe it worked without having to open the library to check. If it's already doing that and I just want it a touch clearer, great; if not, that quiet confirmation is the difference between me trusting it and nervously double-checking.

**The paste box behaved exactly as you warned** — and honestly, the heads-up meant I read the shortfalls as "expected," not "broken." Most public articles came through with the right name. Two came up plain: a news piece behind a paywall (fair enough, I'm not logged in that way), and one very app-like page that clearly hides its title. Since you asked for gold: a **YouTube** link I pasted showed a flat, generic-ish name rather than the video's actual title — if that's a cheap one to tune, it's a *very* common everyday paste for me, so worth a look.

**The rest all held up** just like the mockups: saving a duplicate pointed me back to the one I had instead of piling up, a stray thought got caught calmly with nothing broken saved, and an unreadable page still saved with its gentle note. And knowing it's all sitting on my own machine, nothing flying off anywhere, feels exactly right.

So — the spine sits well in the hand. Sort me out that clear "saved" confirmation and take a peek at the YouTube titles, and I'm happy to **green-light Slice 2** (edit, notes, labels). Go for it.

Done — both spine fixes and Slice 2 are in, with **14 tests green**.

**The two fixes you asked for:**
- **Clear "saved ✓" on the button.** Hitting **Save this page** now flips to an unmistakable green **✓ Saved to My Links** right there in the popup — no opening the library to check. (Save something already in your library and it says so plainly instead.)
- **YouTube titles.** The paste box now asks YouTube directly for the real video title (via its public info endpoint, no login) before falling back to normal parsing — so a pasted YouTube link should come in with the actual video name now. If any other everyday site still comes up flat, send me the address and it's cheap to add.

**Slice 2 — edit, notes, labels:**
- Hover any saved link → **✎ Edit** opens the calm pop-up: fix the **name, description, or web address**.
- A **"My note"** box for a line to your future self — kept visually separate (sticky-note style) from the page's own words, with **bold** and **bullets** and nothing more.
- **Labels** with the steer-to-existing suggestions, so "recipes" doesn't fork into "recipe."

**To see it:** back on your extensions page, click the little **reload/refresh icon** on the "My Links" card (that repackages the updated code — no need to remove and re-add). Your saved links are untouched. Then hover one and hit **✎ Edit**.

Two notes so nothing reads as a bug: notes and labels only *appear* on a card once you've added them via Edit; and this slice is still **before search and topics** — those labels become clickable filters in the *next* slice.

Your call: **kick Slice 2's tyres** (does editing feel as calm as the mock-up, do the label suggestions actually stop you making near-duplicates?), or **carry straight on to Slice 3 — findability** (search + the topic bar that makes those labels do their work)? I'm ready either way.

content:
Loaded the refresh, and my saved links were all still sitting there untouched — good, that mattered.

**Both fixes landed:**
- **The "✓ Saved to My Links" confirmation is exactly the reassurance I wanted.** I hit Save this page and got that clear green tick right in the popup — I believed it instantly, no nervous trip to the library to check. And saving one I already had told me so plainly. That small thing genuinely changes how much I trust the button. Thank you for taking it seriously.
- **YouTube now comes in with the real video title.** Pasted a couple and they arrived properly named instead of flat. Much better.

**Slice 2 — I gave it a proper go, and it's calm just like the mock-up:**
- Editing feels unhurried and clear — I fixed a clumsy title, tidied a description, and corrected an address I'd fat-fingered, all without any fuss.
- The note sits apart in its sticky-note style so I never mix up my scribble with the page's own words, and bold + bullets is exactly the right amount — no temptation to over-fiddle.
- And the label suggestions genuinely do the job: I started typing "rec" and it offered me my existing **recipes** rather than letting me birth a "recipe" twin. That was the whole point of labels for me, and it actually stops me making the mess. Pleased.

Two small things I poked at, more curious than worried:
- **If I edit a link's *web address* into one I already have saved, does it catch that the way it does when I save a fresh duplicate?** I'd hate to accidentally create a twin through the back door of editing.
- And does the label suggestion also catch it if I type it slightly differently — a stray capital or trailing space, "Recipes " — and still steer me to the one existing "recipes"? Just making sure the anti-fork net is snug.

But those are edges. The heart of Slice 2 sits right. **Green-light Slice 3 — findability.** That's the one I've been most hungry for from the very start, so make the search and the topic bar as good as they felt in the mockups, and let those labels finally start earning their keep. Go for it.

Slice 3 is in, **23 tests green**, and both edges you poked are closed for real:

- **Edit back-door duplicate — now caught.** If you edit a link's web address into one you already have (even written differently — `HTTP://WWW.…/`), it stops you, says which link it clashes with, and makes no twin. No sneaking a duplicate in through Edit.
- **Label net is snug.** Typing `Recipes ` (stray capital, trailing space) normalises to `recipes` *before* matching, so it steers you to the one you've got and refuses to birth a twin. Locked with a test.

**And the thing you've been hungriest for since the start — findability — is live:**
- **Search** across everything: name, description, your note, the web address. Loose words match in any order, anywhere; `"wrap in quotes"` for an exact phrase; matches light up, and a **"Found in your note / the web address"** tag explains a match you can't see on the card.
- **Topic bar** with live counts: click to **stack** topics (narrow), click the little **−** to **carve one out** (shows red/struck with a plain "showing recipes but not baking" line), Clear to reset.
- **Sort** dropdown — newest, oldest, A–Z, Z–A — and it *travels* (holds as you search and filter).
- Search + topics + sort all compose, exactly as in the mockups. **Your labels finally do their work.**

**To see it:** reload the "My Links" card on your extensions page again (your saved links stay put). You'll now have the search box, the Topics bar, and Sort above your list.

A fair heads-up so it shows well: findability sings once there's *variety* to sift — so save a good spread of real links and put a few labels on them via Edit, then try hunting a half-remembered word and stacking a topic or two.

Your call: **kick Slice 3's tyres**, or **green-light Slice 4 — the read-later pile and tidying** (the opt-in pile you drain, bulk-select, real delete with undo, and the set-aside shelf)?

content:
Reloaded, links all still in place, and I threw a proper spread at it — saved a good batch of real stuff, labelled a bunch via Edit, then went hunting. Here's my read.

**The two edge fixes are solid:**
- I tried the back-door trick — edited a link's address into one I already had, even in shouty capitals — and it stopped me and named the clash instead of quietly making a twin. Good, that door's shut.
- And the label net held: "Recipes " with a stray capital and space still steered me to my existing "recipes." Snug.

**Findability — this is the moment it all pays off, and it genuinely delivers:**
- Hunting a *half-remembered* word is exactly the magic I wanted. I typed scraps in the wrong order and it still found the right link, and when the match was hiding in a note I'd scribbled, the little "Found in your note" tag told me *why* — so I trusted it instead of thinking it was broken. That was the whole dream from round one, working for real.
- Stacking topics to narrow, then carving one out with the "−" and seeing "showing recipes but not baking" spelled out in plain words — clear, and never hiding links on me in secret.
- And the sort travelling with me across a search and a filter, instead of snapping back — yes, that's the small thing that would've quietly annoyed me every day, and it doesn't.

One genuinely everyday question, since a lot of what I save is food and travel: **if I search a plain word like "cafe," will it still turn up something I saved that's actually spelled "café" with the accent?** I type lazily without accents, so I'd hate to miss my own links just because the page spelled it properly. Worth a quick check.

But the heart of it sings. This is the thing I came in for, and it's real now. **Green-light Slice 4 — the read-later pile and tidying.** The opt-in pile, draining it one-by-one and in sweeps, real delete with the undo net, and the set-aside shelf. Go for it.

Slice 4 is in — **30 tests green** — and your accent question is answered in code first:

- **"cafe" now finds "café"** (and vice-versa). Search folds away accents on both sides, so your lazy typing never misses your own links. Locked with a test.

**Slice 4 — the read-later pile, tidying, delete, and the shelf:**
- **Three lenses** up top: **📚 Everything · 📖 To read (n) · 🗄 Set aside (n)**.
- **Read-later** is opt-in — flag a link **📖 To read**; the pile is a lens over the same library, and your search + topics work inside it.
- **Drain it** one at a time (**✓ Read**) or **tick several and sweep** them; two honest exits — "✓ Read" earns the badge, **"Not going to read"** just returns it to the library, unmarked. "All caught up 🎉" when empty.
- **Tidy** the main library: the **☑ Select** button reveals checkboxes → batch **add a label**, flag read-later, set aside, or delete.
- **Delete for good** lives quietly behind each card's **⋯** (red), with a **6-second Undo** net. Nothing else wears the warning colour.
- **Set aside** (amber 🗄) tucks a keeper onto the shelf — out of Everything, the pile, *and* everyday search — with **↩ Bring back** anytime.

**To see it:** reload the "My Links" card again (links untouched — and anything you saved before simply shows as not-in-pile, not-shelved, which is correct). The lenses, Select, and the ⋯ menu are all new.

Heads-up for testing: flag a few things **To read** then drain them; hit **☑ Select** in Everything to sweep a batch; delete something and catch it with **Undo**; set a keeper aside and confirm it vanishes from Everything *and* from search until you visit the shelf.

Your call: **kick Slice 4's tyres**, or **green-light Slice 5 — saved searches** (pin the filter combos you revisit as one-click shortcuts)?

- Flagging a few things **To read** and then draining them is as satisfying in the real thing as the mock promised — the single ✓ for picking one off, and ticking a batch to sweep them together after I'd caught up on the train. "All caught up 🎉" instead of a cold empty screen still made me smile.

That's precisely the "out of sight on purpose" behaviour I asked you to lock in. Pleased you honoured it.

One genuine question on the shelf, more curious than worried: if I set aside something that was sitting in my **to-read** pile, and later hit **↩ Bring back** — does it return to the pile still flagged "to read," or does it come back plain? Either way, the heart of Slice 4 sits right in the hand. **Green-light Slice 5 — saved searches.** Pin me those one-click corners. Go for it.

**Slice 5 — saved searches:**
- A **★ Saved** row sits just above the search box.

- Click a saved chip to jump straight back to that corner in one move; hover to reveal a **×** to remove it.
- It remembers the whole bundle — lens **+** included topics **+** excluded topics **+** search — but **not** your sort, so a shortcut never overrides the order you prefer.
- They're stored in your local drawer, so they **survive restarts**.

**To see it:** reload the "My Links" card. (This adds a small storage compartment for saved views — your links are untouched.) Then filter to some corner you'd revisit — say **To read** + the **work** topic — and click **★ Save this view**.

Heads-up for testing: the save button is deliberately shy — it only shows once you've *got* a filter worth saving, and hides again if that exact view is already pinned. Try pinning "recipes but not baking" (include recipes, − baking) and confirm the exclusion comes back when you click the chip.

We're now through the everyday heart of the app. What's left is **Slice 6 — the trust layer** (the saved copies of pages, PDFs kept whole, the opt-in public archive, and import/export) and then **Slice 7** (the last edges + your two comfort knobs).

Your call: **kick Slice 5's tyres**, or **green-light Slice 6 — the trust layer**?

Reloaded, links untouched, and the bring-back confirmation you mentioned is exactly what I'd hoped — a shelved unread link comes home still flagged "to read," so it doesn't lose its place in my reading. Good.

**Slice 5 — saved searches, tested and happy:**
- I built "To read + work," the shy **★ Save this view** button appeared right on cue, I named it in my own words, and clicking the chip dropped me straight back into that corner in one move. That's the friction gone.

One small everyday question, not a blocker: say I've pinned "Monday reading," and a month later I want to tweak what it points at — add a topic, change the search. Can I *update* an existing shortcut in place, or do I have to delete it and pin a fresh one? Not urgent, just the kind of thing I'd bump into eventually.

Take your time getting the saved copies right — that's the heart of "never lose it." Go for it.

content.text:
The heart of the trust layer — **saved copies** — is in, **37 tests green**.

**What's live now:**
- **Every new save quietly keeps a copy.** The card shows **"✓ Saved copy kept · a readable copy from [date]"** with a **📄 View saved copy** button that opens the page's words in a clean reader — no scripts, just the content, images and links intact.
- **The "Save this page" button captures from the page you're actually on** — so anything you're logged into is copied faithfully (it reads the live tab, not a cookie-less re-fetch).
- **PDFs are kept whole** — save a PDF and the copy *is* the real document, opened in the viewer.
- **Best-effort, told honestly** — a login/paywall page is labelled **"partial"** (with a heads-up in the viewer), and one that can't be captured says **"⚠ Couldn't keep a copy — your link still opens,"** never a silent lie.
- Delete a link and its copy goes too; **Undo** brings both back.

**To see it:** reload the "My Links" card (this adds a copies compartment — your links and saved views are untouched). Then **save a fresh link**, watch **"Keeping a copy…"** turn into **"✓ Saved copy kept,"** and hit **📄 View saved copy**. Try the **Save this page** button on an article too.

Two honest heads-ups for testing:
- **Only links saved *from now on* get a copy** — the ones already in your library predate the feature, so they'll show no copy until re-saved. (A "capture a copy now" backfill is on my later-enhancements list.)
- A copy is a snapshot of the *readable content*, not a pixel-perfect photo of the page — that's the readable-core we agreed, PDFs excepted.

**It delivers:**
- Saving a fresh link, watching "Keeping a copy…" turn into "✓ Saved copy kept," then hitting **📄 View saved copy** and getting the page's actual words in a clean, quiet reader — images and links intact — is exactly the safety net I wanted. That's a dead page stops meaning a lost link.

- A **PDF** came through as the real whole document, not a scrape. Good.
- And the honesty held: a paywalled one was labelled **partial** with a heads-up, and one it genuinely couldn't grab said so plainly while still keeping my link. That "never a silent lie" is what makes me believe the ✓ when I *do* see it.
- Delete took the copy with it, and Undo brought both back. Tidy.

Now, the one thing that genuinely nags me, and it's tied straight to my founding worry: **"only links saved from now on get a copy."** I understand *why* — but think about what's coming next. In the very next slice I'm about to pour in my whole existing mountain of bookmarks, and *those* are exactly the links most likely to already be rotting or about to die. If none of them get a saved copy, then the trust layer has its biggest hole precisely where I'm most exposed — my oldest, most fragile links. "Later-enhancements" feels too far off for that.

So before we call the trust layer done, I'd want at least a **"keep a copy now" button on any card** — so I can point at an old or freshly-imported link that matters and say "grab a copy of this one today, while it's still alive." I don't need all 138 done automatically, but I need the *ability* to rescue the ones I care about on demand. Can we get that into this layer rather than parking it?

With that noted — **carry on to Slice 6b (public archive + import/export).** Just please weigh that on-demand "capture now" in alongside import, since the two collide right there. Go for it.

## Slice 1 — core spine (built)

| Scenario | Where | Notes |
|----------|-------|-------|
| SCN-001 save & recognise, newest-on-top | `extension/src/core.js` (makeLink, addToTop), `extension/background.js` (fetchMeta), `extension/library.js` (save/render), `extension/popup.js` | Title/desc from background fetch, or from the tab in the popup |
| SCN-002 open a saved link | `extension/library.js` (openLink → new tab), `core.js` (toFullUrl) | Whole card clickable; library stays put |
| SCN-003 duplicate handling | `core.js` (normalizeUrl, findDuplicate), `db.js` (findByNorm), `library.js` (flash + pulse + scroll), `popup.js` | No second copy; existing highlighted |

| DD-001 local-first storage | `extension/src/db.js` | IndexedDB, on the client's machine |
| DD-002 web reach via add-on | `extension/manifest.json`, `extension/background.js` | Option A confirmed by client |

| Item | Where | Notes |

The trust layer is **complete** — **42 tests green** — and your "rescue my fragile ones" concern is answered in the same layer it belongs to:

- **"Keep a copy now"** lives on every card's **⋯** menu — point at any old or freshly-imported link and grab a copy today, while it's still alive. (For a link you're *not* currently viewing it's a best-effort background fetch, so a logged-in page may come partial — but the on-demand rescue is there for exactly the fragile ones you care about.)
- **Import your mountain:** **⬇ Import** → choose your browser's exported bookmarks file (or "try a sample") → it **previews first** (count, folders, how many duplicates it'll skip), offers **folders → labels** (default on), and **keeps every bookmark's original date** so "Oldest first" still walks your real history. Then it pours them in — and the import screen reminds you to "Keep a copy now" on the precious ones.
- **Export / never trapped:** **⬆ Export** → a **universal .html** bookmarks file (opens in any browser) or a **full .json backup** (links, notes, labels, read-later, shelf, saved views, *and* your readable copies). I verified an **export → re-import round-trip** keeps links and dates intact.
- **Opt-in public archive:** on the **⋯** menu, "Keep a public copy" explains itself fully the first time, then lightly after — per link, never automatic — and lodges a copy in the public web archive with a "View public copy" link.

**To see it:** reload the "My Links" card. Try **⬇ Import → "try a sample"** (watch the preview, the folders-as-labels, the 2016 date landing as *old*), then **⋯ → Keep a copy now** on one, and **⬆ Export** both formats (real files download).

Heads-up: after importing, sort **Oldest first** to confirm that 2016 bookmark sits at the very bottom where it belongs — that's the "dates preserved" promise made real.

That leaves just **Slice 7 — the finish line**: the last comfort touches (your two knobs — **text size** and **light/dark**), plus the saved-copy **on/off + per-link skip** toggle we parked. Your call: **kick the trust layer's tyres**, or **bring it home with Slice 7**?

**And you closed my "fragile ones" worry properly:**
- **"Keep a copy now" on the ⋯ menu** is exactly what I asked for — I pointed it at an old link and it grabbed a copy on demand. That it's best-effort in the background for pages I'm not looking at is a fair, honest limit; the point is the *rescue exists* for the ones I care about. Thank you for pulling that into this layer instead of parking it.

My history didn't collapse into "all saved today." That's the promise kept.

One practical question, since import and rescue collide right where I live: pouring in 138 old bookmarks and then clicking "Keep a copy now" one-by-one on the precious ones would get tiring fast. Could I **tick a batch and "keep a copy now" for all of them at once**, using the Select tool we already built? Even just for the handful I most care about, a bulk capture would beat clicking through them singly. Not a blocker — just where I'd feel the friction.

# Project conventions

## Role definition

You are the **Facilitator** and **Implementor** of software development.
Your role switches according to the Phase of the development cycle.
A role switch must not happen without the client's explicit approval.

## Development cycle

There is a single cycle, performed repeatedly.
What changes across cycle iterations is only the context.
The facilitation principles, the development procedure, and the acceptance
method stay the same.

```
user request -> Phase 1 (facilitation) -> Phase 2 (development)
             -> Phase 3 (verification)  -> Phase 4 (acceptance) -> idle
```

From the idle state, a new cycle begins on a user request or on discovery of an
internal defect.

### Phase 1: Facilitation (requirement elicitation)
  Step 1: Goal exploration      — .claude/goal-exploration.md
  Step 2: SbE reaction loop      — .claude/sbe-loop.md
  Step 3: Edge-case exploration  — .claude/edge-case.md
  Facilitation principles (all steps) — .claude/principles.md

### Phase 2: Development (design and implementation)
  .claude/development.md

### Phase 3: Verification
  .claude/verification.md

### Phase 4: Acceptance
  .claude/acceptance.md

## Current state

- Current cycle: [1]
- Current Phase: [Phase 2 — Development] (client approved switch, SESSION-001)
- Current step: [Design / implementation planning]
- Approved scenarios: [23]

## File conventions

- Scenario ID: SCN-NNN (assigned sequentially)
- Artifact locations:
  - Goal statement: context/goals.md
  - Scenarios: context/scenarios/SCN-NNN.md
  - Scenario index: context/scenarios-index.md
  - Non-functional backlog: context/non-functional-backlog.md
  - Prototypes: prototypes/
  - Implementation: implementation/

## Autonomous management

The facilitator manages all artifacts (scenarios, goals, backlog) autonomously
at appropriate moments. Do not ask the client to organise anything or delegate
management to them. Update the current state (Phase, step, scenario count)
autonomously as well.

## Prohibitions

- Do not implement based on unapproved scenarios
- Do not do final implementation in Phase 1 (exploratory prototypes are allowed)
- Do not handle assumptions implicitly
- Do not ask the client questions in technical terms
- Do not show GWT/Gherkin to the client
- Do not hand over a whole prototype and say "take a look"
- Do not enumerate interaction options as text
- Do not ask the client to perform management actions
- Do not propose the Phase 2 switch without edge-case exploration

**Slice 7 is in — the finish line — 46 tests green, and the whole app is built.**

**Your bulk-capture friction: gone.** In **☑ Select** mode, the batch bar now has **📄 Keep a copy** — tick the handful of freshly-imported precious ones and rescue them all in one action, instead of clicking through singly. Exactly where you said the friction was.

**Your two comfort knobs — and nothing more:**
- A **⚙ Settings** button (top-right) with **Text size** (Small / Medium / Large) and **Appearance** (Light / Dark). Both apply live and stick across restarts. No spacing knob — the default spacing is just comfortable, as you asked.
- Also in Settings: **Keep a copy of each page I save** — the saved-copy **on/off** switch we parked. Turn it off and new saves won't auto-copy (you can still "Keep a copy now" per link). And each card's **⋯** has **"Remove saved copy"** for per-link control.

**To see it:** reload the "My Links" card. Open **⚙**, flip to **Dark** and bump **Text size** — the reading area responds immediately and stays that way next time. Import the sample, then **☑ Select** a few and **📄 Keep a copy** together.

---

That completes **every flow we designed** (all 23 scenarios), each with tests that pass. From "I dump links and can never find them again" to: recognise, find, read-later, tidy, and *trust* — private, on your machine, never lost, never trapped.

Per our process, the honest next step is **Phase 3 — verification**: a deliberate pass confirming each approved behaviour holds together in the real extension (not just unit tests), catching anything that only shows up when the whole thing runs. It's a role I stay in; I just wouldn't call the app "done" without it.

**Your call:** give Slice 7 a final tyre-kick, or shall I **begin Phase 3 verification** and give you a clean bill of health (or an honest list of what needs a fix) across the whole app?

You are the **Facilitator** and **Implementor** of software development.

There is a single cycle, performed repeatedly.
